title: What AI Actually Is: Module Quiz

cards.prompt: Which of these **learn from examples**, and which just **follow rules** someone wrote?

items.label: An online shop's "you might like" list

cards.explanation: A microwave timer and a spreadsheet's adding follow exact rules. Turning speech into text and suggesting things you might like have endless variety, so they **learn from examples**.

cards.prompt: The model calls the mini basketball a tennis ball. Choose which examples to train on, so it gets **every** test ball right.
cards.explanation: Every basketball the model learned from was big, so the mini one sat closer to the tennis balls. Adding the **small basketball** shows it that basketballs can be small too. Taking the tennis balls out would break the tennis ball test.

cards.prompt: A model learned to spot dogs from photos taken **only in daylight**. What will it most likely get wrong?

options.text: The photos it was trained on
Dogs in photos taken at night
Nothing: the kind of photos doesn't matter

cards.explanation: A model only knows what it was shown. It never saw a dog at night, so night photos are where it will slip up, like the yellow apple. Adding night photos to its training data would help.

cards.prompt: A café trained a burnt-toast spotter on lots of toast photos, each labelled "burnt" or "fine". Then they used it in the kitchen straight away. It keeps calling dark rye bread burnt, and nobody noticed until customers complained. What went wrong?

options.text: They skipped trying it on new toast before using it for real
They should have used it in the kitchen first, then labelled photos
The labels confused it: it would learn better from unlabelled photos
Rye is just too dark: trying it out first wouldn't have shown anything

cards.explanation: The steps are collect, label, train, **test on new examples**, then use. Trying it on new toast, including darker breads, would have shown the mistake before customers did. Labels are how it learns, so they're needed, and using it for real comes last.

cards.prompt: You're writing questions for a quiz night with an AI helper.

steps.text: The AI confidently tells you the name of the world's highest volcano. Teams will argue about every answer. What do you do?

choices.consequence: It might be right, but it might not. AI answers are predictions, and confidence doesn't make them true.

choices.text: Check it in a trusted source first
choices.consequence: Exactly: important facts get checked with a source you trust.

choices.text: Ask the AI to promise it's right
choices.consequence: It may well promise, but it can't be sure its own answer is right, so a promise doesn't make it true.

cards.explanation: An AI's answer is a prediction. For anything important, **check it with a trusted source** before you rely on it.

cards.prompt: A company uses AI to sort 500 job applications. Who should make the final call on who gets the job?

options.text: A person, who checks the AI's suggestions and is responsible
The AI, because it's faster and never gets tired or grumpy
A manager, who hires the AI's top pick without reading the others
The AI, because it learned from thousands of past job choices

cards.explanation: Who gets a job is a **big decision about people**. AI can help sort applications, but its picks are predictions and can be wrong, so a person checks them, decides and is responsible. A manager who just rubber-stamps the AI's top pick isn't really deciding. Speed and lots of examples don't change that.

cards.prompt: A team is building an app that sorts photos into cats and dogs. Match each part of their work to the word for it.

pairs.left: 500 photos of cats and dogs to learn from
The word "cat" written on one photo
The program that now sorts new photos by itself
"Dog": its best guess about a new photo

cards.explanation: The 500 photos are the **training data**; "cat" on one photo is a **label**; the program that sorts new photos is the **model**; and its guess about a new photo is a **prediction**.
